name: Benčnon / Bench'
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Wedekind, Klaus. 1983. A six-tone language in Ethiopia: Tonal analysis of Benč non (Gimira). Journal of Ethiopian Studies 16: 129-156.
catalog_locator: JES 16 (1983), p. 133 ('A Sketch of the Segmental Phonology of Benčnon'), p. 134 ('A Description of the Tone System of Benčnon'), p. 147 ('Synchronic and diachronic aspects of tone change'); the scan of the author's PDF
catalog_quote: Benčnon has about forty phonetically different segments and several suprasegmentals (Tone, length, laryngealization, nasalization); but of all these, only tone and 33 segmental phonemes (28 consonants, 5 vowels) are distinctive. [p. 133] ... Each syllable of the Benčnon language has one of six contrasting tonemes, normally carried by the nucleus V or N (vowel or syllabic nasal) of the syllable. Five of the tones are level or 'register' tones, and the sixth is a rising glide. ... So there are five distinctive relative pitch levels, but six tonemes. Each of them has been found to occur on any one of the vowels or nasals, and each of them occurs in all positions of the word and on all major word classes. [p. 134] ... Another cause for a shift to tone 4 may be the re-interpretation of stress in loan words as 'shifted' high tone: Loans tend to have a rising tone pattern, such as in za³yit⁴ 'oil', or ma³kin⁴ 'car'. This conforms with the stress on final syllables in Cushitic and Omotic languages. [p. 147]

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File opened: (29-page author PDF of JES 16, 1983; no text; scanned in and per-page ocr1983/). Page mapping checked from printed folios: p. 6 = JES p. 133, p. 20 = JES p. 147. Both pages rendered (page render) and read as images. The quoted sentences are there verbatim: p. 133, section 'A Sketch of the Segmental Phonology of Benčnon', third paragraph: 'Benčnon has about forty phonetically different segments and several suprasegmentals (Tone, length, laryngealization, nasalization); but of all these, only tone and 33 segmental phonemes (28 consonants, 5 vowels) are distinctive.'; p. 147, diachronic section on tone 4: 'Another cause for a shift to tone 4 may be the re-interpretation of stress…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Bench is a lexical tone language with five level tones plus one rising toneme; Wedekind's suprasegmental inventory for Bench is tone, length, laryngealization and nasalization, with tone the only distinctive one -- stress is not part of the inventory and no word-stress placement rule is given. The only stress remark is diachronic/contact: final-syllable stress of loanwords (Amharic, Cushitic) is re-interpreted as a high tone (tone 4) on the final syllable. Wedekind 1985b (p. 110) adds the family-level generalisation 'Cushitic languages have phonetic or phonemic stress, Omotic languages, tone'. Lexical items are overwhelmingly monosyllabic (Wedekind 1985: 888, loans are 'the very small set of Bench' polysyllabics'), so a stress rule would be near-vacuous.
new_statements.exceptions: Loanwords (disyllabic) carry a 3-4 rising tone pattern reflecting source-language final stress; no synchronic stress exceptions stated.
new_statements.domain_note: Word/citation-form level; Wedekind's data are elicited citation forms and short phrases from one Addis Ababa speaker (1980-81). No explicit sentence of the form 'Bench has no stress' was found; the reading is inferred from the suprasegmental inventory and the tone-only characterisation.
new_statements.identity_note: Wedekind's 1983 data are from a single Benchnon speaker at Addis Ababa University; Rapold (2006, per Wikipedia summary) treats Benchnon, Shenon and Mernon as mutually intelligible varieties of one language = benc1235. Names in the literature: Bench, Benchnon, Benč non, Gimira, Bench'.

sources.note: Bench described as a five-level (six-toneme) tone language; p. 133 lists the suprasegmentals as tone, length, laryngealization, nasalization (no stress) with only tone distinctive; p. 147: stress of Amharic/Cushitic loans is re-interpreted as a high tone 4, 'conforms with the stress on final syllables in Cushitic and Omotic languages'; the 1983 map (p. 132) puts Benchnon among the '5 Tones' Omotic languages. No word-stress rule for Bench.
